processing: Oxidised more heavily than modern Dong Ding, around 30–40% with properly red leaf edges, ball-rolled and then roasted in several sessions over weeks with rests between, to a medium level that cooks the sugars without charring.
harvest_season: Spring and winter leaf; the roasting is done over the following months and the tea is usually released a few months after the harvest.
appearance_dry: Tight, dark olive-brown half-balls with a dull sheen and a smell of dried fruit and warm sugar.
appearance_liquor: Amber to reddish gold, thick-looking and clear; the 'red water' of the name.
appearance_wet: Green-brown leaves with clearly red edges, supple and whole, not blackened.
taste_profile: Dried longan, apricot and honey with a cocoa-like depth, a thick, smooth texture and a sweetness that rises in the throat and stays.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, a reasonable dose and steady steeps; it goes ten infusions, growing sweeter and more mellow. A clay pot on a cool evening suits it better than a quick gaiwan session.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest and roast: typically the spring or winter leaf of a stated year, roasted over the following months and rested at least a few weeks before release, and good makers hold it back for a year or more because it improves. Sealed and dry it keeps for years, and some lots are sold as five- or ten-year-old tea; a lot of the best Taiwanese aged oolong started life as Hong Shui.
description:
Hong Shui, 'red water', is the old way of making Dong Ding and, for many Taiwanese tea drinkers, the proper one. From the 1970s, as the fashion swung to green, lightly oxidised rolled oolong, Dong Ding from Lugu moved with it. The older manner, with the leaf oxidised until the edges were properly red and then charcoal-roasted, was recreated in the 1980s by the poet Ji Ye with Lugu farmers and tea makers, and shown as Hong Shui oolong in 1987; the amber-red liquor gave it its name, and the style has been in demand since.

The leaf is Qing Xin oolong, withered longer and tossed harder than modern Dong Ding to reach roughly 30 to 40 percent oxidation, pan-fired, ball-rolled and then roasted in several sessions over weeks, with rests between so the heat penetrates without charring. The roast is a tool rather than the point: it cooks the sugars that the fuller oxidation produced, and a well-made Hong Shui tastes of fruit and honey first and fire second.

In the cup, expect dried longan, apricot and honey, a cocoa-like depth, a thick, smooth texture and a sweetness that rises in the throat and stays. It is easy to brew: boiling water, a reasonable dose and steady steeps, and it goes ten infusions, growing sweeter and more mellow. It is a tea for a clay pot and a cool evening rather than for a quick gaiwan session.

It is sold by harvest and roast: typically the spring or winter leaf of a given year, roasted over the following months and rested at least a few weeks before release, and good makers hold it back for a year or more because it improves. Check the wet leaf: real Hong Shui shows green-brown leaf with clearly red edges, while leaf that is uniformly dark or blackened is a heavy roast on under-oxidised tea and will taste of charcoal rather than fruit.

Store it sealed and dry and it keeps for years; some of the best Taiwanese aged oolong started life as Hong Shui.
history:
Tea growing in Lugu is recorded from the Jiaqing years of the Qing dynasty, using Qing Xin oolong brought from Fujian. The earliest Taiwanese oolong was made rather like Wuyi rock tea, more oxidised and heavily charcoal-fired, with a reddish cup. Under Japanese rule the fashion moved to the Anxi method and a paler, half-ball tea, and from the 1970s fragrant green oolong took over, Dong Ding included.

The name itself is modern. In the 1980s the poet Ji Ye worked with contract farmers and traditional tea makers in the Dongding, Fenghuang and Yonglong villages of Lugu to recreate the old manner of making, and presented the result as Hong Shui oolong in 1987. It helped revive charcoal-roasted oolong more widely.
